title: Officer felt he had to shoot, police say
article: The Calgary Police Service is always looking for alternatives to using lethal force, but new tools on the market are unproven and expensive, says Staff Sgt. Rick Rudd.
When police face an armed suspect threatening to harm a hostage or officer, as happened Saturday at a downtown pharmacy, they have only a handful of options ranging from negotiation to lethal force.

The hostage situation at the TD Square quickly escalated until the first officer on the scene felt he had to use his firearm against the knife-wielding man. He fatally shot Arthur George Provencal, 34, in the head.
Const. Rick Parent, an officer in Delta, B.C., who has studied police shootings, says Vancouver-area police are experimenting with new alternatives.
One is the taser, a 50,000-volt, dart-shooting stun gun that incapacitates the target. Its range is about five metres. The other is a bean-bag shotgun with twice the range.
"Both are effective," he said. "Both can disable a suspect. They give an officer another option."
The Calgary Police Service has a few bean-bag shotguns, which are used for crowd control and prolonged standoffs.
It doesn't have tasers. They're considered too experimental and too expensive. Parent said tasers cost up to $700 each.
Rudd, who is in charge of Calgary's support section, said the department will wait for the results of an RCMP study of the device.
"If tasers were found to be an appropriate use of force, we would do everything in our power to equip our people with them."
Rudd said equipping officers with more equipment might be too much of a burden. He added that use of force in Calgary already includes pepper spray and batons, in addition to firearms.
Meanwhile, Provencal's family is objecting to the media portraying him solely as a career criminal.
"I'd like the public to understand that he has family who will miss him and always love him dearly," nephew Mark Saikaly wrote in a letter to the Herald.
"Like any family, we are grieving. My only comfort is to know that publicly his final moments on Earth do not define him as a human, which should never be the case. ...
"Beneath all the pain, suffering and confusion was a man just like anyone else, and that is how I will remember him."
Provencal had served time for assault and armed robbery.
